common_name: Busy Bee Chaste Tree (JBG 19002 Dwarf Compact Vitex)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring after frost danger passes, siting in full sun with well-drained soil; Busy Bee (sold under this trade name) was bred for a naturally tidy, well-branched dwarf habit that needs little pruning to stay compact.

directions: Busy Bee was selected from an open-pollinated Vitex breeding program for its dense, lacy palmate foliage and naturally rounded, well-branched form that stays far smaller than a typical seedling chaste tree without any pruning. Grape-purple flower panicles emerge in loose spikes above the foliage from midsummer into fall, drawing steady bee and butterfly traffic over an extended bloom window. Plant in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; once roots are established the shrub shrugs off heat, humidity, and short dry spells with minimal supplemental water. A light shaping cut in late winter is usually enough to refresh flowering wood, though plants that suffer hard freeze dieback will resprout readily from the base.

common_name: Rock Steady Chaste Tree (Extended-Bloom Purple Vitex)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Rock Steady (sold under this trade name) was bred and trialed for a markedly longer bloom season than older vitex selections and rewards a sunny, open site with the heaviest flowering.

directions: Rock Steady was trialed against a field of established vitex cultivars and stood out for blooming several weeks to months longer, holding its light purple, candelabra-shaped flower spikes on new wood from late spring all the way through fall. It builds an upright, somewhat narrow habit compared to older wide-spreading selections, making it a fit for tighter side-yard or foundation plantings as well as open borders. Grow in full sun and average, well-drained soil, watering new plants regularly until established and thereafter relying on rainfall except during extended drought. Deer generally leave the aromatic foliage alone, and an annual late-winter cutback to a low framework keeps the plant dense and maximizes the following season's flower count.

common_name: Flip Side Chaste Tree (Purple-Backed Hybrid Vitex)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun with well-drained soil; this hybrid, sold under the trade name Flip Side, was bred specifically to bring cold-hardier, purple-backed foliage into the tender V. trifolia line.

directions: Flip Side is a deliberate cross of tender Vitex trifolia with hardy V. agnus-castus, combining the olive-green, purple-backed foliage of its tropical parent with far better cold tolerance, surviving as a woody shrub through zone 7 winters and returning from the roots even further north. Arching branches carry fragrant, deep violet flower spikes repeatedly from summer into fall, and the two-toned leaves flash purple whenever wind turns them over, giving the plant its name and a second season of interest beyond bloom. Site in full sun and well-drained soil, since heavy or soggy ground shortens its life; established plants tolerate heat and dry spells with little intervention. Prune hard in late winter after the coldest weather has passed to remove any dieback and encourage the densest new flowering growth.

common_name: Short Stack Chaste Tree (Dwarf Sterile Negundo Vitex)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in full sun to light shade; Short Stack (sold under this trade name) was bred from thousands of seedlings for a naturally dense, mounded dwarf form and sterile flowers, so it needs no deadheading and stays compact without shearing.

directions: Short Stack is a sterile dwarf selection of the Asian chaste tree species Vitex negundo, growing a foot or so a year into a tight, rounded mound of dense, dark green foliage rather than the loose, leggy habit typical of straight-species negundo. Because its blue-purple flower spikes are sterile, the plant channels energy into repeat flushes of bloom from midsummer through the first hard frost instead of setting seed, and deadheading is unnecessary. It performs best in full sun on well-drained soil with regular moisture during establishment, then tolerates considerable heat and short dry spells once mature; in colder parts of its range it may die back to the crown in hard winters and should be cut to the ground in late winter to resprout vigorously. Its small stature suits foundation plantings, mixed borders, and mass plantings where full-size vitex would overwhelm the space.
